https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/ma.text: McHenry County Marine veteran, 48, identified as woman killed in Fox River DUI boat crash "She would go above and beyond for anyone, there was no one like her, the most selfless and kind person you would ever meet," said Michelle Macias, Jablonska's sister. By Randy Gyllenhaal and Izzy Stroobandt • Published July 28, 2026 • Updated on July 28, 2026 at 10:26 pm BOOKMARKER NBC Universal, Inc. The woman killed by a speeding boater on the Fox River is remembered by family as a selfless and kind Marine veteran. Randy Gyllenhaal reports. The 48-year-old woman who was struck and killed by a speeding boater on the Fox River over the weekend is remembered by her family as a selfless and kind U.S. Marine veteran who served her country after immigrating to Chicago from Poland. Magdalena Jablonska was out on the Fox River on Saturday with her family when 45-year-old boater Richard Stevenson slammed into the vessel they were on from behind at 80 mph, according to authorities. Stevenson was both drunk and speeding when he crashed into them, prosecutors said. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE Jablonska was killed in the crash and her dog and fiancé were both injured. "She would go above and beyond for anyone, there was no one like her, the most selfless and kind person you would ever meet," said Michelle Macias, Jablonska's sister. Macias said Jablonska joined the Marines "straight out of high school" and "never [did] anything for herself, always for everybody else." Jablonska was a big fan of dogs and often "loved the shelters for the puppies," her family said. They are now raising money for animals in the wake of the devastating loss and hope that Stevenson will be held accountable in court. "We are giving our hopes and faith they will do right by her so nobody else gets hurt," Macias said. Local Northwest Indiana 20 minutes ago ‘Stay put': Entire town in northwest Indiana without power after severe storms Severe Weather 42 minutes ago ‘We've got a mess': Rolled over semis, downed power lines block part of Indiana interstate Stevenson, who worked for the prominent Bolingbrook-based Stevenson Crane Company that is owned by his family, is facing charges of aggravated DUI and reckless homicide after the crash, records show, and prosecutors say his blood alcohol content was twice the legal limit when he sped his high-powered pontoon in a slow zone. Prosecutors called him a "ticking time bomb" because of his history of DUI charges dating back more than 20 years, including two previous DUI convictions, three reckless driving convictions, three fleeing and eluding police convictions and four misdemeanor speeding convictions, according to court records. They also said witnesses described how he had picked up a bucket of Fireball whisky bottles and was drinking them as he drove. He allegedly stopped later at a bar for two more shots. They say that after the crash, Stevenson admitted to another witness that he was drinking and that his life was over. He stayed on the scene and was later taken to a hospital where he allegedly refused blood and urine tests, according to prosecutors. “We offer our sincerest condolences to the victims’ families and loved ones. Yesterday, Richard Stevenson's employment with the company in the equipment sales department was terminated. He held no leadership role," Stevenson Crane Company said in a statement. Stevenson was ordered to be detained until trial , and his next court date is set for August. Lake County Sheriff John D. Idleburg released a lengthy statement on Tuesday regarding the crash, stating in part: "Like so many in our community, I am frustrated and saddened by the reckless, dangerous, and inexcusable and preventable actions of a boater on the Fox River whose actions claimed one life and critically injured another person last weekend. The victims were people simply enjoying time on our recreational waterways. Our hearts go out to the victims and their families, and we are hoping for the recovery of the person critically injured." https://www.jns.org/news/antisemitism/is.text: “The murders cannot be undone. Denying the victims’ remembrance adds another grave wrong: It continues the effort to erase them from history.” The International March of the Living on Friday called on the German town of Heidenau to reverse its decision to ban installations of Stolpersteine memorial stones for Holocaust victims, saying that its implication is to continue the effort to “erase them from history.” A Stolpersteine is a four-inch concrete cube bearing a brass plate inscribed with the names and life dates of victims of Nazi extermination or persecution. The decision made on Thursday by the council of the German town, situated in the state of Saxony near Dresden, must be a “wake-up call,” the March of the Living said. The nonprofit organization is dedicated to bringing people from around the world to Poland and Israel to study the Holocaust. “The Nazis murdered Jews and tried to erase their names, their communities and their place in history. Eighty-one years after the end of the war, elected officials in Germany have voted to prevent more of those names from appearing on the streets where the victims lived,” the statement read. The organization noted that similar attempts are being made elsewhere in Germany, which raises the question: “Are political interests being allowed to push the memory of Nazi victims out of public life?” Israeli Ambassador to Berlin Ron Prosor wrote a German-language post on X, saying that he is “ashamed.” “In Germany in the year 2026, a city council decides to no longer allow any new Stolpersteine. Every person has a name. A world. A story. It is precisely this memory that is being erased here. Whoever erases the victims from the past erases the past itself,” he said. “Germany needs a clear firewall against antisemitism—from the right, from the left, and from Islamist circles. Without exception.” https://x.com/Ron_Prosor/status/2103443715222122671The world’s largest decentralized monument The political factions behind the ban are the Christian Democratic Union, considered center-right, and the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the right-wing party that secured earlier in September historic electoral victories in two German states, German News Service (DW) reported. The initiators of the ban argue that while commemorating the Holocaust’s victims is important, “passersby walking over [the memorial cubes] or even stepping onto the names of the victims” does not accomplish this, the report continued. The council voters offered to honor the victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead. The Stolpersteine project began in 1990 at the initiative of German artist Gunter Demnig. Today, 128,000 memorial stones are installed across 31 countries, most of which can be found in Germany, and they are recognized as the world’s largest decentralized monument, according to DW.
